title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Monday; 1/7 of week lost. Past weeks with partial closures show ~13% sales reduction.

drivers.name: Price increase (6% higher)
drivers.evidence: Same price point ($4.08) in 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05 led to 3–5 units (29–49% of baseline). Noise-adjusted price effect at this level: ~x0.75.

adjustment.analysis: The store is closed Monday, removing 1/7 of the week's potential sales. The price is 6% higher, which likely reduces demand. Past price increases to $4.08 (e.g., 2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 3–5 units, far below baseline. No promotions or events are scheduled. The classical model's neutral suggestion is unconvincing: it ignores the price increase and closure. The closure implies a 13% sales loss (1/7). The price rise likely reduces sales by ~20–30% based on past behavior. Combined, these drivers suggest a strong downward adjustment.

brief:
PRODUCT: Candy Corn Bag | category Candy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-18 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.3 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 23.5 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 18.6

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
